newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turk parliament cuts maximum period of custody.
newsitem.headline: Turk parliament cuts maximum period of custody.

text.p: Turkey's parliament on Thursday approved a law shortening the maximum period a suspect can be held in police custody without charge to 24 hours from four days, deputy speaker Yasin Hatiboglu said.
For human rights groups, the length of police detention in Turkey has for a long time been a key issue and has drawn criticism from Europe.

"The draft law is accepted," Hatiboglu said after MPs voted in favour of the law, which still has to be approved by Turkish President Suleyman Demirel and published in the Official Gazette before it comes into force.

Under the previous law, groups of more than three suspects could be held for eight days. They will also be subject to the new 24-hour limit, but the maximum period of their detention will be extendable to seven days on a judge's decision.
The text of the law requires that detainees have constant access to legal representation and stipulates that the trial of an inmate must begin within four months of his initial detention.
Human rights activists say the initial period of detention is when suspects are most at risk from the torture. Activists say torture is systematic in Turkey.
The European Parliament has blocked millions of dollars of aid to Turkey, partly as a result of its human rights record.

In Turkey's nine emergency rule provinces, the maximum detention period without charge under the new law will be cut to one week from 30 days previously. But for groups of more than three this can be extended to ten days on the order of a state prosecutor.
For those suspected of crimes endangering state security, tried in Turkey's State Security Courts, the maximum period of custody will be reduced to 48 hours from 15 days.
A prosecutor can lengthen the maximum period for groups suspected of such crimes to four days and a judge can extend this further to seven days.

The law envisages taking the offence of hijacking out of the jurisdiction of the State Security Courts and placing it under the authority of normal criminal courts, meaning potentially shorter sentences for those found guilty of the crime.

A hearing was scheduled to be held on Friday in the trial of nine pro-Chechen activists, who seized a Black Sea ferry last year. They face maximum sentences of 34 years on charges of hijacking and forming a terror group.
The nine men -- six Turks, two Chechens and an ethnic Abkhaz from Georgia -- seized the 3,838-ton ferry Avrasya in January 1996 in protest at Russian treatment of Chechen rebels.
